### Question 1

Read a shopping list out loud: "bread, peanut butter and jelly." Three items, or two, with peanut butter and jelly as one sandwich filling? The serial comma is the fence that keeps the last two items from fusing. Two things tell you it is the serial comma and not some other comma: the list has at least three members, and the comma sits right in front of the final "and" or "or."

### Question 2

Think of three traffic signals. A period is a full stop, a comma is a yield, and a semicolon is the rolling stop in between: both halves could be separate sentences, but you want the reader to feel them as one thought. Run the swap test before you use one. Replace the semicolon with a period and read both pieces aloud; if either piece cannot survive alone, you needed a comma or a conjunction instead.

### Question 3

An apostrophe either grabs or fills. It grabs when something is owned (*the nurse's stethoscope*) and it fills the gap where letters were squeezed out (*do not* becomes *don't*). It never announces that there is more than one of something. That single distinction settles the hardest pair in English: *its* is the grabbing pronoun, already possessive with no gap to fill, while *it's* has a gap where the *i* of *is* used to be.

### Question 4

Commas around a description work like parentheses that whisper "by the way." "My cousins, who live in Ohio, called me" means every cousin lives in Ohio and every one called. Drop the commas and "my cousins who live in Ohio called me" means only the Ohio branch phoned. Try the deletion test: if lifting the clause out leaves the noun still pointing at the right people, the clause is extra and takes commas; if the noun goes vague without it, the clause is doing identifying work and takes none.

### Question 5

A colon is a drumroll. The words in front of it make a promise, and the words after it pay it off. That is also the source of the one rule people get wrong: the drumroll only works if the setup is already a whole sentence. Test it by reading only up to the colon. "The chart listed three vital signs" stands alone, so the colon is earned; "The three vital signs are" does not, so the colon has to go.

### Question 6

Picture two loaded wagons. A comma is a piece of string: fine for hitching a small trailer such as a phrase, but it snaps under two full sentences. Real hitches are a comma teamed with *and, but, so*, or a semicolon, or a period that parks them separately. "It rained, we stayed inside" is string. "It rained, so we stayed inside" is a hitch, and so is "It rained; we stayed inside."

### Question 7

A hyphen is tape that binds two words into one label. Taped, *small-bowel* names a place, the small intestine. Untaped, *small* floats free and could be sizing up the problem instead. The same tape decides lunch in "a man-eating fish" versus "a man eating fish." One useful check: the tape belongs only when the bundled words sit in front of the noun, which is why we write "a well-known author" but "the author was well known."

### Question 8

Read the apostrophe as a doorway, with the owner always standing to its left. In *patient's* the doorway opens right after one patient, so one person owns the chart. In *patients'* it opens after the whole group, so the group does. Build the possessive in that order and the mark will land in the right place: write the owner first, exactly as it is spelled, then add the doorway, then add an *s* unless the owner is a plural that already ends in *s*. So you get the nurse's badge, the boss's office, and the children's ward, but the patients' lounge.

### Question 9

Some words are players in the action and some are just the person you are talking to. The comma is the rope line keeping Grandma in the stands. Remove the rope and she walks onto the field and becomes part of the action, in this case dinner. The same rope explains "Thanks, Dad" versus "Thanks Dad," and it works on both sides of a name: "Grandma, let's eat" and "Let's eat, Grandma, before the soup cools."

### Question 10

A comma can say either "next item" or "same thing, named again," and a reader who sees just one of them has no way to choose. Adding the comma before *and* makes the shape unmistakably a list, so the accidental adoption disappears. When you write a series in which any item could be read as a description of the item before it, insert the serial comma every time; that is the situation the mark exists for.

### Question 11

Imagine three ways to deliver an aside. Whispering behind your hand is parentheses, saying it with a hand wave is em dashes, and saying it in your ordinary voice is commas. All three are still asides, and the sentence stands up if you cut them. So the marks are volume knobs, not switches that decide whether the words matter. One practical consequence: if the sentence collapses when you remove the enclosed words, the problem is not which mark you picked, it is that the words never belonged in an aside.

### Question 12

Punctuation has ranks, like the levels of an outline. Commas are the lower rank and semicolons the higher one, and normally commas are enough to divide a list. But when the items themselves contain commas, every mark looks alike and the reader loses count, so you promote the dividers to semicolons and let the commas keep working inside each item. Watch for this pattern whenever a list holds names with credentials, cities with states, or dates with years.
